segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for "what" or "that"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Que. And what was the word for "to buy"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comprar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comprar, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if we wanted to say something like, "That you bought it is not my problem," "That you might have bought it is not my problem," "The fact that you bought it is not my problem," we can just start with que,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and put the verb in the mood tense, and we get this feeling, "the fact that you may have bought it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We're doing the same thing in English. "May have" - with this "may" we are getting some mood.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's start, speaking informally, "That you bought it / That you may have bought it".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So comprar becomes compraron, comprara, compraras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Que compraras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Don't forget your "it", just because you're concentrating so much on the verb, huh?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah. Que lo compraras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "...is not my problem."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No es mi problema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Que lo compraras no es mi problema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Maybe you want to say something like, "That you told him is not my problem."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So to tell, we can use decir, "to tell" or "to say", or contar we saw as well. Contar means "to count" or "to recount". So let's use contar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "That you told him / The fact that you told him is not my problem," speaking informally still.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Que contaras... Que le contaras no es mi problema.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Que le contaras no es mi problema. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In English, I should say - although I have this London English, so so often I don't say - I should say, "If I were you."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, "I was" is the normal past tense, no, from "to be"? "I was".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we change "was" to "were" to get the past mood tense in English, "if I were you," hypothetical past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In Spanish, whenever we speak about the past hypothetically after si, after "if", we will use the mood tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for example, what was the verb "to be able to", "can", related to "power"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Poder.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Poder. Now if you want to make the "they" form in the past, "they could / they were able to", there's a slight change.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The pod- that you would be left with after taking -er away from poder turns to pud-.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pud-.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "they were able to" using the point in the past?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pudieron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pudieron, good. So from this base we can form the mood tense. So if you wanted to say something like, "If I could, if I could cook, I would cook."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "if I could"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si pudiera...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "...to cook"? Or "to kitchen"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cocinar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Si pudiera cocinar, "I would cook".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So to find "would", you must look back at "I would like / it would please me".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me gustaría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So there you have your "would". So, "I would cook"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cocinaría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Si pudiera cocinar, cocinaría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, "If I could cancel it, I would"? So, "If I could cancel it, I would cancel it."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si pudiera cancelarlo...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I would", so, "I would cancel it".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo cancelaría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Si pudiera cancelarlo, lo cancelaría. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to have"? The "to have" that we use to go into the past?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Haber. Now when haber goes into the point in the past, that first bit hab- of haber, when you take off your -er, it changes for the point in the past. It becomes hub-, H-U-B.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "they had" using the point in the past, going from haber and this hab- of haber will become hub- when we make the point in the past?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hubieron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hubieron, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we can say, "If you had told me it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So speaking informally, "If you had told me it" - how would you say that? "If you had told me it"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si me lo hubieras contado...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Si me lo hubieras contado, "I would have gone." So, "If you had told me, if you had told me it, I would have gone."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now we need "would have". We leave everything else at the door. So how do we get "would have" from haber?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habría.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. The E falls away, habría. So, "I would have gone"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habría ido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So all together, "If you had told me it, if you had told me it, I would have gone."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si me lo hubieras contado, habría ido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Si me lo hubieras contado, habría ido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "If we had known, we would have gone." "If we had known, we would have gone."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si hubiéramos sabido...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "...we would have gone."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habríamos ido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is "to see"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ver.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ver. And what is "they saw", point in the past?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vieron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vieron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "my house"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mi casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mi casa. "Your house", informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tu casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tu casa. Do you remember how to say "his house", "her house", "your house" formally, "their house"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Su casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Su casa, good. So how would you say, "If you saw their house..."?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "If you saw their house..."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si vieras su casa...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Si vieras su casa...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, "If you saw it, you would understand it"? Let's speak formally. "If you saw it, you would understand it,"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: speaking formally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si lo viera, comprendía... comprendería.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comprendía is the past is the tense, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The line in the past, very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Si lo viera, lo comprendería. Or we could use entender, which also means to understand,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Si lo viera, lo entendería.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I should mention that there also exists an alternative form for the past mood tense, the past subjunctive, with -ase or -iese. So you may hear hablase instead of hablara,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: or entendiese instead of entendiera, comiese instead of comiera, comiésemos instead of comiéramos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But how much that alternative form is used really depends on the dialect. The main way, the most common way of using the past subjunctive is the one that we've learned here,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and there's no difference between the two in meaning. They are just two versions of the same tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you don't need to worry about using hablase instead of hablara for example, but you would need to recognize it if you hear it or read it somewhere.
